item.content:encoded:
It’s been an exciting September for Austin Wells off the field — and the Yankees hope there will be a thrilling October on it to match.
The Yankees catcher got engaged to girlfriend Caroline Nielson earlier this month, according to photos she shared of the proposal on Instagram.
Nielson posted Wednesday photos of a touching beach scene with Wells down on one knee before the couple embraces.
The “forever and ever” caption suggests that the proposal took place Sept. 3 — an off day for the Yankees between series in California against the Angels and Padres.
They also included a photo of their daughter, Lucy, as part of the joyous moment.
Several significant others of Yankees teammates were quick to toast the couple in the comments section.
“My heart!!!!! Let’s get these two married!!! 🥹🥹🥹♥️♥️♥️♥️” wrote Ava O’Connor, who is dating outfielder Spencer Jones.
“The best off day in the history of off days,” wrote Carlos Rodon’s wife, Ashley.
“SCREAMING CRYING,” wrote Ben Rice’s girlfriend, Sara Falkson.
It is unclear when the couple first started dating. They announced that Nielson was expecting a child last November in one of the first public signs of a relationship.
Before the big day, Wells has an important postseason in front of him.
The 27-year-old catcher has somewhat rebounded from a miserable start to the season, pushing his average up to .185 after dipping down to .150 in July.
Wells, who is respected by the Yankees for his skills behind the plate, will likely be a mainstay in the lineup during the postseason.

That will begin next week when the Yankees in all likelihood will take on the Red Sox in a best-of-three wild card series in The Bronx.
Wells did have perhaps his biggest moment in pinstripes when the rivals met last season in the same round, driving home the game-winning run with an eighth-inning single in Game 2.
The Yankees evened the series that night and went on to win Game 3 the following evening.
Now, Wells and the Yankees will look for an even deeper postseason run with Nielson no doubt cheering him on from the stands.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees 6, Angels 3, and for eight and a half innings Wednesday night at Angel Stadium, this one looked like it might stay 1-1 into the parking lot. Cam Schlittler made sure it didn't get out of hand. Austin Wells made sure it never got to an 11th.
Wells' two-out, bases-loaded single in the 10th was the whole game in one swing -- a 1-2 fastball from Luke Murphy that found right field, scoring two and flipping a tossup into a laugher. By the time the inning was over, the Yankees had scored five runs on four straight singles and taken the rubber match of the series, 2-1.
The Turning Point
Extra innings started with Amed Rosario parked on second, the automatic runner, and it took a while to cash him in. José Caballero singled to send him to third. Jazz Chisholm Jr. walked to load the bases. Luis García Jr. popped out for the second out, and for a second it looked like the Yankees might strand the whole mess (they'd left 14 men on base by night's end, which tells you something about how stubborn this offense had been all night).
Then Wells got to Murphy. Two runs scored, Chisholm to third. Cody Bellinger singled him home. Trent Grisham singled Wells home. Ben Rice singled in Bellinger. Four hitters, four singles, five runs, and the Angels never got the third out they needed to escape it.
Star of the Game: Schlittler Rewrites the Record Book
Before any of that happened, Schlittler spent eight innings quietly making history. Two hits. One run. Nine strikeouts. Zero walks. Ninety-nine pitches, 71 of them strikes -- the kind of start where you check the line twice because it doesn't look real for a guy facing a lineup with Mike Trout in it.
That was the 19th time this season Schlittler has allowed a run or fewer in a start. That's a new Yankees single-season record, passing the mark of 18 shared by Ron Guidry's 1978 Cy Young season, Whitey Ford in 1964, and Jack Chesbro all the way back in 1904. Good company. Better yet, Schlittler's still adding to it.
He didn't get the win (no decision, if you're scoring at home), because the Yankees' bats needed extra innings to back him up. He also didn't seem to care. That's usually the sign of the right kind of pitcher.
Detmers Made Him Earn It
Give the Angels' Reid Detmers his due, too. Seven innings, six hits, one earned run, eight strikeouts of his own -- the only damage against him a ground-rule double by Rosario in the fourth that scored Bellinger. For seven innings, this was a legitimate pitchers' duel between two guys who deserved a better final line than "no decision."
Vaughn Grissom's solo homer off Schlittler in the seventh tied it at 1-1 and set up the standoff that lasted until the 10th blew it open.
Boone's Bullpen Math Worked, Barely
David Bednar came in for a scoreless ninth -- one hit, three strikeouts -- and got the win when the Yankees broke through an inning later, which is how it works even if Bednar didn't throw a single pitch in the inning that decided it. Michael Fulmer took the 10th with a five-run lead and made it interesting, giving up a two-run homer to Moisés Ballesteros that scored the Angels' own automatic runner, Wade Meckler. Fulmer got the next two outs anyway. A laugher stayed a win, which is really all that matters in the box score.
Yankees take the series 2-1 after dropping the opener 1-10 on Monday, and they move to 80-60, three and a half back of the Rays with a month to play. San Diego's up next.
Jimmy writes the Bronx Pinstripes game recap after every Yankees game. Beat-reporter pacing, fan's heartbeat. He calls opposing players by last name and has no patience for dead-air innings.

Cody Bellinger is out of the New York Yankees lineup for Wednesday night's game against the Tampa Bay Rays, but no injury has been reported.
With the top American League wild-card spot secured and Aaron Judge sidelined, the open question is how many at-bats Bellinger takes into a best-of-three series that starts in six days, most likely against the Boston Red Sox.
José Caballero moves into left field against Rays right-hander Mason Englert, according to CBS Sports. The site found nothing pointing to a physical problem and characterized the absence as a pre-playoff day off.
The timing follows a cold stretch. Bellinger opened September by hitting .373 through his first 14 games of the month, then managed just three hits in his next 20 at-bats.
He managed to come through on Tuesday. His fourth-inning, two-run homer off Nick Martinez, his 17th of the season, was the only scoring in a 2-0 Game 1 win before Tampa Bay took the nightcap of a doubleheader 6-1 and clinched the American League East.

Yankees Rest Plan Includes Cody Bellinger
After the doubleheader, manager Aaron Boone singled out Bellinger, catcher Austin Wells and outfielder Spencer Jones as regulars due for rest over the final week, according to Yankees beat writer Gary Phillips.
"As best we can, we'll get ourselves sharp. They're real games, so we're playing, but I definitely will pick some spots to get some guys down. Some of our leverage guys in the 'pen, we want them pitching, but we'll be very selective in how we do it," Boone said as quoted by MLB.com's Bryan Hoch.
Gerrit Cole starts Wednesday, and Cam Schlittler follows Thursday before a three-game series against the Baltimore Orioles closes the schedule, according to Hoch.
At 90-67, New York holds the No. 4 seed and will host the No. 5 seed in the Wild Card Series opening Sept. 29, according to MLB.com. The Boston Red Sox, at 84-73, are the likeliest opponent.
Judge will not be part of it. Boone said the captain has a "moderate" right calf strain and is not expected back for that round, according to Hoch.
"Missing Judge, it hurts. We all know he's the best hitter in the game. For us in here, our mindset is, we're going to have to find a way," Bellinger said, as quoted by Hoch.
Bellinger Career Resume
Bellinger's September line sits at .338/.351/.581 with five homers and 14 RBI, according to Yardbarker. He has appeared in 76 playoff games, hitting 10 homers and driving in 37 runs.
Bellinger was born July 13, 1995, in Scottsdale, Arizona. The Los Angeles Dodgers drafted him in the fourth round in 2013, straight out of Chandler's Hamilton High School. He won National League Rookie of the Year in 2017 and NL MVP in 2019, when he hit .305 with 47 homers.
His path also runs through a 2020 World Series title with the Dodgers and two seasons with the Chicago Cubs. New York acquired him in a December 2024 trade and, after a 2025 season of 29 homers and 98 RBI, re-signed him in January to a five-year, $162.5 million contract that gives him two opt-out chances and full no-trade protection, according to Bronx Pinstripes.
Limited to 130 games by a 25-game injured-list stint for a left hamstring strain, Bellinger is hitting .268 this season with 17 homers, 73 RBI and 12 stolen bases. His career totals stand at 242 home runs and 768 RBI.

item.content:encoded:
Updated Yankees projected Wild Card Series roster without Aaron Judge
NEW YORK - Here was the scenario these Yankees hoped to avoid, but couldn't - a triumphant Tampa Bay Rays team, celebrating their AL East title on Bronx turf.
"They've put together a fantastic regular season to earn that,'' said manager Aaron Boone, after the Rays' 6-1 victory in Tuesday's nightcap of a split doubleheader at Yankee Stadium.
"Hopefully, we get another crack at them.''
That would be in a best-of-five AL Division Series, but only if the Yankees advance from a best-of-three Wild Card series, which they'll host - likely against the rival Red Sox.
With that Wild Card opponent in mind, here is our updated version of a Yankees 26-man playoff roster (12 pitchers, 14 position players), for a series that would begin on Tuesday, Sept. 29.
Rosters can be altered before each postseason round. Injured players can be replaced in-series (pitcher for pitcher, position player for position player) but the injured player is ineligible for the next playoff series.
Projected Yankees pitchers (12)
Starters (3): RHPs Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole; LHP Max Fried.
Relievers (9): RHPs David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Will Warren, Michael Fulmer, John Schreiber; LHPs Ryan Weathers, Tim Hill, Brent Headrick, Carlos Rodon.
On the bubble: RHPs Clarke Schmidt.
Also available: RHPs Luis Gil, Elmer Rodriguez, Yerry de los Santos, Bradley Hanner, Carlos Lagrange; LHP Ryan Yarbrough.
Currently injured: RHPs Fernando Cruz, Angel Chivilli, Kervin Castro.
Analysis: Would the Yanks start anyone but Schlittler in Game 1?
Well, nothing's been firmly stated about the first round rotation, though Schlittler - the odds-on choice for the AL Cy Young Award - would be on normal rest for the opener.
Cole (Wednesday) and Schlittler (Thursday) will make their final regular season starts during this Rays series, though Boone mentioned limiting both starters in these tune-ups for postseason.
In the bullpen, Schmidt's recent bout of biceps cramping wasn't fully resolved as of Tuesday; he was due to be re-examined after a throwing session.
It's possible that even a slight setback takes Schmidt out of consideration for an important playoff spot, moving Michael Fulmer off the bubble and on the roster.
Rodon's eight shutout innings in Tuesday's doubleheader opener was his best effort, during an impressive stretch drive.
He'd be certain to start Game 1 or 2 of a Division Series vs. the Rays, but the Yanks might need his services - in some capacity - to advance vs. Boston, so he's now included here.
Projected Yankees infielders, utility/DH (9)
Infielders (7): Luis Garcia Jr., 1B; Paul Goldschmidt, 1B; Ben Rice, 1B-DH; Jazz Chisholm Jr., 2B; George Lombard Jr., SS; Anthony Volpe, 2B-SS; Ryan McMahon, 3B.
Utility players: (2): Jose Caballero, IF-OF; Amed Rosario, 3B-2B.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: Max Schuemann.
Analysis: Garcia and McMahon are slumping at the wrong time, while Chisholm - who just returned off the IL (right thumb sprain) on Tuesday - has this week to find his rhythm again at the plate.
But that trio of lefty hitters might all be starting on the bench against Boston, which could employ three lefty starters against the Yanks.
That puts Caballero in play as a third base option, with the veteran Goldschmidt (.997 OPS vs. lefties) at first base, the rookie Lombard at short, and Volpe recast as a second baseman.
Projected Yankees outfielders (3)
Cody Bellinger, Spencer Jones, Heliot Ramos.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: Jasson Dominguez.
Currently injured: Aaron Judge, Trent Grisham.
Analysis: That's a thin outfield without Judge, whom the Yanks are not planning to have for at least the Wild Card series - per Boone - due to the captain's "moderate'' right calf strain.
It's increasingly unlikely that Grisham (strained hamstring) is available, too, by next week, and that presents a danger considering Ramos' defensive deficiencies.
For that same reason, Dominguez is on the outside. Mostly, the Yanks need the potent right-handed bats of Ramos (who has found his hitting groove) and Rosario to combat Boston's lefty pitching.
Caballero could find himself pressed into outfield duty, too.
Without Judge, "it's going to be super tough on us,'' said Ramos. "But we're going to go forward, for sure.''
Yankees' projected catchers (2)
Austin Wells, Ali Sanchez.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: J.C. Escarra.
Analysis: Wells has been a better offensive presence after a brutal first half, and Sanchez has learned the staff and he earned much praise from Rodon for his contribution to Tuesday's game one win.
Boone has kept the Cole-Wells pairing together, and you'd still anticipate Wells getting starts vs. Boston's lefty starters throughout this opening series.

The New York Yankees saw the Tampa Bay Rays claim the AL East crown at Yankee Stadium on Tuesday night. A 6-1 loss in the nightcap of a doubleheader split ended whatever remained of the division chase and confirmed what had felt inevitable for weeks. The Yankees are headed to the Wild Card Series.
The sting of the celebration was real. So was the pragmatism that followed it. With five regular season games remaining and the postseason less than a week away, manager Aaron Boone's focus has already shifted to October.
His assessment of one pitcher in particular made that clear.
Boone's Comments on Fried
Max Fried will not pitch again in the regular season. Tuesday's start against the Rays was his final tuneup before the playoffs.
"I think he looks great," Boone said. "I thought he was really good tonight. He threw the ball well. His curveball was really, really good tonight. Cutter was there. For the most part, was filling up the strike zone really well."
Fried's night unraveled in the seventh when a bunt play went sideways and three runs came in. Before that, he had been efficient and sharp. Boone saw a pitcher who is ready for October, not one who got tagged for four runs.
"He managed contact really well. I thought he was efficient," Boone said. "He's in a good place ready to go. Looking forward to seeing him out there in the postseason now."
Managing the Final Five Games
With the standings locked in, Boone outlined how the Yankees will approach the rest of the week. The priority is keeping players sharp without wearing anyone down.
"Getting guys ready, picking some days for some guys to get off," Boone said. "We're the real game. So we're playing. But I will pick some spots to get some guys down."
Cody Bellinger and Austin Wells are candidates for rest days. Spencer Jones may get a day to manage. Boone also mentioned experimenting with defensive positions and being selective about when leverage relievers pitch.
The balance is delicate. The games do not matter in the standings. The rhythm and preparation matter for everything that comes after.
Final Word for the Yankees
The division belongs to Tampa Bay. The Yankees know it. They watched the celebration and walked off their own field.
What happens next is the only thing that counts. Fried is ready. Cole and Schlittler are lined up. The rotation has three arms capable of winning a postseason start.
The Wild Card Series begins next week, with a Red Sox series in the Bronx the most likely outcome. Boone's message on Tuesday was simple. His team is not done. The pitching is in place. Now it is time to prove it matters.

NEW YORK (AP) — Drew Rasmussen allowed his only hit in the seventh inning and struck out 11 as the Tampa Bay Rays beat the New York Yankees 6-1 on Tuesday in the second game of a day-night doubleheader to clinch their fifth AL East title.
The Rays (96-61) secured home-field advantage throughout the American League playoffs and took their first division crown since 2021, when they won 100 games. Tampa Bay also earned AL East championships in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season along with 2010 and 2008, when the team had its first winning season after entering the league as an expansion franchise in 1998.
Yandy Díaz hit two-run single off reliever John Schreiber in the seventh and had another two-run single in the ninth for his AL-leading 175th hit. Tampa Bay opened a six-game lead over the second-place Yankees (90-67) with five to play.
In the opener, Carlos Rodón allowed three hits in eight sharp innings as New York delayed Tampa Bay's division celebration with a 2-0 victory.
Taylor Walls started the three-run seventh with a bunt single against Max Fried (5-5) when first base was left uncovered. Ryan Vilade hit an RBI groundout in the third after Díaz’s flyball moved runners to second and third.
Rasmussen (16-5) was nine outs from joining Matt Garza as Tampa Bay pitchers with a no-hitter when he gave up a leadoff double to Heliot Ramos on his 97th pitch. Garza held the Detroit Tigers hitless at Tropicana Field on July 26, 2010.
After allowing Ramos’ hit to left field, Rasmussen got the next two outs before walking Jazz Chisholm Jr. on a full count. Kevin Kelly entered and permitted rookie George Lombard Jr.’s RBI single before retiring Austin Wells on a groundout.
Rasmussen threw a career-high 114 pitches, 72 for strikes. He threw first-pitch strikes to 17 of 24 hitters and notched his fourth career double-digit strikeout game.
Rasmussen allowed one hit for the fourth time this year. He also yielded just one hit in six innings against the Yankees on April 12.
Cam Booser and Bryan Baker pitched an inning apiece to finish the three-hitter.
Fried allowed four runs and six hits in 6 2/3 innings.
The Yankees were held to three hits or fewer for the 13th time this year.
Up next
Tampa Bay RHP Ian Seymour (9-7, 4.38 ERA) opposes New York RHP Gerrit Cole (9-9, 3.63) on Wednesday night.

Rays' Drew Rasmussen loses no-hit bid in 7th inning on leadoff double by Heliot Ramos
NEW YORK (AP) — Tampa Bay right-hander Drew Rasmussen lost a no-hit bid against the New York Yankees on Tuesday night when Heliot Ramos led off the seventh inning with a double.
The Rays, attempting to clinch the AL East title, had a 4-0 lead when Ramos lined a 1-2 sinker to left field, two pitches after hitting a foul ball down the right field line.
Before losing his no-hit bid, Rasmussen had 10 strikeouts and has thrown 93 pitches, 59 for strikes through six innings.
Matt Garza is the only Tampa Bay pitcher to throw a no-hitter. Garza no-hit Detroit on July 26, 2010, at Tropicana Field.
Rasmussen ended the sixth inning by getting New York's Cody Bellinger on a flyball to right field.
Rasmussen walked Austin Wells with one out in the third and ended the inning by striking out Ben Rice on a high fastball. The 31-year-old issued a leadoff walk to Cody Bellinger and ended the fourth by striking out rookie Spencer Jones with a fastball.
Rasmussen got consecutive strikeouts on rookie George Lombard Jr. and Austin Wells to finish the fifth at 78 pitches.
The Rays can claim their fifth AL East title with a victory and took a 1-0 lead on Ryan Vilade’s groundout in the third against Max Fried. They added three in the seventh on a bunt single by Taylor Walls and a two-run base hit by Yandy Diaz.
The Yankees have been no-hit eight times. The last was a combined no-hitter by Houston’s Cristian Javier, Hector Neris and Ryan Pressly on June 25, 2022, at Yankee Stadium.

item.content:encoded:
When Aaron Judge is healthy, he’s the most dangerous hitter in baseball. Sometimes I get alarmed at how uncontroversial a statement that is; ours is a sport that so frequently humiliates those who make such sweeping, unequivocal judgments as those.
But the empirical evidence is what it is. Judge has played 150 or more games in a season four times in his career. In those four seasons, he’s led all position players in WAR four times and led the league in wRC+ three times. He’s been named AL MVP three times and finished second once, ahead of some real doozies: Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer year, Bobby Witt Jr.’s 10.5-WAR campaign in 2024, Shohei Ohtani’s best pitching season — in fact, a healthy Judge is the only thing that’s ever trumped a healthy Ohtani in an MVP race.
So again, it’s not uncontroversial to say that when Judge is healthy he’s the best hitter in the world. He has not, however, always been healthy. Least of all this season, when he missed three months with a broken rib. And now, the single-season AL home run king is back on the IL with a calf strain. The timing could not be worse.
Judge last played on Wednesday, leaving open the option to activate him on Sunday for the final game of the regular season. That seems like a theoretical concern at the moment rather than a practical one. Our Matt Martell was at Yankee manager Aaron Boone’s pregame media availability on Tuesday morning, where Boone illustrated the inadequacy of a return-to-play timeline at this point in the season.
“We’re planning on [Judge] not being a part of [the Wild Card Series],” Boone said. “You hear all the time with injuries, we give ranges: two to four weeks, four to six. They’re ranges for a reason. We’re at a point in the year where, obviously, we’d push it a little bit if that was in play, but that’s a week away. I’m not expecting it, but I’m not ruling it out either.”
That’s the problem. A range of two weeks in recovery time isn’t a big deal in a six-month season, but even one week is twice as long as the Yankees’ entire first playoff round. And muscle injuries can be finicky to begin with — you go to bed one night feeling fine and wake up the next morning with weakness or stiffness.
For what it’s worth, the Yankees are technically still alive in the AL East race as of this writing, but you can forgive Boone for speaking as if the division is already lost.
Either way, in order to speed things along, Judge received a platelet-poor plasma (PPP) injection on Monday, not to be confused with a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection.
Now, apparently having read The Magic School Bus Inside the Human Body as a child is not a sufficient qualification to perform surgery on live patients. At least, that’s what the police told me. But anyone who’s read that book can tell you the makeup of human blood: Red blood cells, which carry oxygen; white blood cells, which fight infection; platelets, which stop bleeding and heal wounds; and plasma, which is the broth all the other stuff floats around in.
PRP injections are a pretty common treatment for sports injuries, but taking the healing bits out of plasma seems kind of counterintuitive. Sort of like a vodka-poor screwdriver. But evidently PPP contains high levels of fibrinogen, which is itself a healing agent. Ms. Frizzle didn’t cover fibrinogen, but sure, I’ll buy it.
Unless the PPP works an actual miracle, though, it looks like the Yankees are going to have to navigate at least the first round of the playoffs without their best player.
And even if Judge does return — either in the Wild Card round or later, if the Yankees advance — I’d caution against assuming that we’d be seeing the best of him right off the proverbial bat. For starters, 99% of star athletes in history are going to try to force their way into the lineup for the playoffs regardless of whether they’re actually healthy.
To say nothing of the fact that Judge can be streaky. This is the nature of Judge’s unusual skill set; there are 1,073 hitters in major league history with at least 5,000 career plate appearances. Judge is the only one of those who’s produced one of the three true outcomes (home run, strikeout, walk) in more than half of his career plate appearances. (I’d like to express my immense gratitude to Adam Dunn, who has a career TTO% of 49.9, for making this fun fact possible.)
Living on the extremes, as he does, Judge will have weeks where he homers every night, and others where he goes 1-for-20 with 12 strikeouts. But you live with it because, over a long enough timeline, it works out heavily in his favor. Among hitters with at least 5,000 career plate appearances, Judge has the third-highest career wRC+, trailing only Babe Ruth and Ted Williams. If you wanted to go further than “best hitter now” and anoint Judge the best hitter ever, leaning heavily on the argument that quality of competition increases over time, you’d have a credible case.
But that’s not what the Yankees got out of Judge this year. In 66 regular-season games, he’s hit .241/.360/.511, with his highest strikeout rate (29.8%) since 2019 and lowest wRC+ (141) since 2020. In seven games since he returned from his rib injury, Judge was just 4-for-23 with one home run, one walk, and 13 strikeouts.
I’ve done enough of these injury reaction posts to figure out that they’re not really about the guy who got hurt, but about the teammates he’s leaving behind.
And I don’t want to underrate the value of Judge — even the version of Judge that has a 141 wRC+, rather than a 200 wRC+ — but the Yankees have done OK without him.
In the weakest American League field in decades, the Yankees are one of only two teams with a winning percentage of .550 or better. Entering their doubleheader with the Rays on Tuesday, the Yankees are still first in the AL in home runs (216) and second in runs scored per game (4.60). Even without Judge (or Giancarlo Stanton, for that matter), their lineup has plenty of beef.

Ben Rice in particular has been absolutely terrific this season. He’s fourth among qualified AL hitters in wRC+ and third in both home runs and runs scored. The Astros have AL MVP frontrunner Yordan Alvarez in their lineup; apart from him, is there any hitter in the AL bracket who’s been Rice’s equal this year? Maybe Junior Caminero? Willson Contreras, if you value OBP over raw power? Even if you’re being charitable, it’s a short list.
Now, past Rice, things get interesting, because if you want to talk about the Yankees’ offensive depth, you have to be able to hold multiple ideas in your head at once.
As of Tuesday morning, the Yankees have 11 hitters with double-digit home runs this season, which is tied for the most in the league. That’s just counting players who have hit 10 or more home runs in pinstripes, and the Yankees brought in substantial reinforcements midseason. Luis García Jr. has just seven homers for the Yankees but 30 overall. Heliot Ramos has four home runs in 32 games and 13 overall, with 20-plus in each of his previous two seasons. George Lombard Jr. has just five home runs in 37 major league games, but he hit 12 dingers in 78 minor league games before he got called up.
Count all this up and the Yankees have more hitters with at least decent pop than they can fit on the roster at once.
At the same time, Rice is the only Yankee with 20 home runs in pinstripes this year. So while this lineup is short on automatic outs, if Judge is out, there’s a massive drop-off after Rice.
If you take Judge out of the picture, Cody Bellinger is second on the Yankees in wRC+, at 119. The Rays don’t have anyone with 100 or more plate appearances and a better wRC+ than Rice this season, but they have four hitters (Caminero, Yandy Díaz, Jonathan Aranda, and Victor Mesa Jr.) with 100 or more plate appearances and a better wRC+ than Bellinger. So do the Rangers (Justin Foscue, Josh Jung, Joc Pederson, Wyatt Langford). The Astros have Alvarez, plus Isaac Paredes and Jeremy Peña. The White Sox have Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami, and Tristan Peters.
As good as Rice has been, the Yankees’ lineup looks concerningly pedestrian without Judge. If you aren’t already a FanGraphs Member, please consider becoming one; it’s the only way to get trenchant original analysis like this.
The good news is that Judge’s calf injury runs counter to the rest of the team’s injury luck. Carlos Rodón, who missed almost three months with an elbow injury earlier this year, dominated the Rays in eight scoreless innings in Game 1 of a doubleheader on Tuesday. The same day, the Yankees activated Chisholm, who’d spent two weeks on the IL with a sprained thumb. Clarke Schmidt just returned from Tommy John surgery last week, and while he suffered biceps cramping in the bullpen on Sunday, it appears to be a minor setback. Trent Grisham remains a question mark for the start of the playoffs as he recovers from a hamstring injury, but his prognosis also looks good.
Judge is as important to the Yankees as any two or three other players put together, but with a healthy and deep rotation and Rice leading the way offensively, they’re not in bad shape. The remainder of this roster could easily survive and advance through a weaker AL bracket, setting the stage for a dramatically timed Judge return in mid-October. Like Kirk Gibson, only bigger.
Michael is a writer at FanGraphs. Previously, he was a staff writer at The Ringer and D1Baseball, and his work has appeared at Grantland, Baseball Prospectus, The Atlantic, ESPN.com, and various ill-remembered Phillies blogs. Follow him on Twitter, if you must, @MichaelBaumann.

item.content:encoded:
It felt like Aaron Judge was returning at the perfect time. A September return following a three-month stint on the IL gave Judge enough time to find his timing before the postseason. Unfortunately, Judge suffered another injury before the playoffs even began, hurting his calf in a game against the Minnesota Twins. The New York Yankees hoped it'd be minor, but it was serious enough for the team to place its captain on the Injured List. Now, it sounds as if a return for the Yankees' first postseason series is a long shot at best.
A "moderate grade" calf strain is serious enough for Yankees manager Aaron Boone to proceed as if his best player won't be active at all for the Wild Card series. That is an insanely difficult blow for a Yankees team that, with Judge, is as good as any in a weak American League. For the Yankees to advance to the ALDS and potentially get their captain back, they'll need to rely on this projected lineup below.
What the Yankees lineup could look like without Aaron Judge
Judge is an instrumental piece in the Yankees' lineup for a couple of reasons. First, he's the best hitter in the sport when healthy. That obviously matters. Second, Judge is one of the few right-handed bats on this roster. He provides much-needed balance that, without Judge, the Yankees lack.
| Position | Player |
|---|---|
| Ben Rice | DH |
| Cody Bellinger | LF |
| Heliot Ramos | RF |
| Luis Garcia Jr. | 1B |
| Spencer Jones | CF |
| George Lombard Jr. | SS |
| Jazz Chisholm Jr. | 2B |
| Austin Wells | C |
| Jose Caballero | 3B |
This lineup still has some good pieces in it. Ben Rice has had a breakout year, Cody Bellinger is a well-rounded star, and trails only Yordan Alvarez and Pete Crow-Armstrong, the AL and NL MVP favorites, with a .532 slugging percentage. If Jazz Chisholm Jr. can return from the IL looking like the player he's capable of being, the Yankees can score runs.
The problem, though, is that six of the nine hitters in this lineup are left-handed, and most of them are much better against righties than lefties. The Yankees will use guys like Paul Goldschmidt and Amed Rosario against left-handed pitching, but having Heliot Ramos, who has a .672 OPS since being acquired by the Yankees at the deadline, in the No. 3 hole against righties isn't ideal. The Yankees don't have much of a choice with Judge out, though.
Ultimately, with Judge out, this is a team heavily reliant on lineup platoons. It'll be on Aaron Boone to try to push the right buttons in order to get this offense, which has been remarkably inconsistent without Judge, to score runs against (likely) a potent Boston Red Sox pitching staff.
Aaron Judge injury update: Can the Yankees expect their star to return?
What's most frustrating about the Judge injury update is that we have no idea what the injury is. The Yankees, for whatever reason, keep information regarding injuries, particularly to Judge, extremely close to the vest, making it difficult to know when or even if Judge will be back. All we know is that Judge is dealing with what Aaron Boone deems a "moderate" strain.
That doesn't sound good, especially for a player who has had trouble with the same right calf in the past. In the shortened 2020 season, Judge attempted to return from a calf strain in a couple of weeks, but wound up re-aggravating the injury, pushing his return back several weeks. Calf injuries and other soft-tissue ailments are not to be messed with, and can lead to a major setback if rushed through.
Plus, if the injury was minor, wouldn't the Yankees be quick to tell the world that? I'd love to say Judge is a lock to return at some point, but even if the Yankees were to advance to the ALDS, given how little we know and how tricky returns can be from calf injuries, it's probably wishful thinking to assume he'd be back right at the start of a potential ALDS, which is the last thign any New York fan wants to hear.

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK -- Ha parecido inevitable que la lucha por el Este de la Liga Americana se decidiera esta semana en el Bronx.
Los Rays han encabezado la división más competitiva de Grandes Ligas durante gran parte de la temporada y no han cedido el primer lugar de la tabla desde que recuperaron la cima el 27 de junio.
Pero los Yankees siempre han estado ahí, amenazando y luego retrocediendo. Pero nunca han estado lo suficientemente lejos como para restarle importancia a lo que podría suceder esta semana.
Pues bien, llegó el momento.
Los Yankees recibirán a los Rays para una serie de cuatro juegos en el Yankee Stadium, comenzando con una doble-cartelera el martes. Gracias a la magnífica estadía de los Rays en casa y a la serie perdida por los Yankees en Phoenix frente a los Diamondbacks, la pregunta ahora es cuánto tiempo más seguirá viva esta lucha.
Los Rays llegaron a Nueva York con 6.0 juegos de ventaja en la división y apenas siete encuentros por disputarse. Una victoria de Tampa Bay eliminará a los Yankees de la lucha por la División Este y los dejará asegurados en un puesto del Comodín de la Liga Americana. Entonces, para que los Yankees tengan alguna posibilidad, deberán completar una barrida de cuatro partidos en tres días.
¿Lo que está en juego? Como dijo una vez Gerrit Cole: “Es mucho”. Entremos en materia.
¿Qué está en juego?
Rays: Ganar apenas un juego les garantizará a los Rays su primer campeonato del Este de la Liga Americana desde el 2021, otorgándoles un pase directo a la Serie Divisional y la ventaja de localía tanto en esa ronda como, si avanzan, en la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana. También necesitan una sola victoria para asegurar la serie particular contra los Yankees.
Yankees: El piloto Aaron Boone reconoce que será una “tarea muy difícil” evitar que los Rays celebren con champaña en el Bronx, pero eso es exactamente lo que pretenden hacer. Empezaron la temporada buscando cambiar la narrativa, después de quedarse cortos ante los Azulejos el año pasado. En cambio, están a punto de tener que conformarse nuevamente con un premio de consolación y verse obligados a ganar una serie al mejor de tres juegos.
¿Cómo están alineadas las rotaciones?
Rays: Enviarán a sus mejores dos abridores al montículo para la doble-cartelera del martes. Primero será el derecho veterano Nick Martínez, líder del clubhouse y su fuente más confiable de innings. Tampa Bay tiene marca de 22-7 esta temporada en los juegos iniciados por el cubano-estadounidense. Después, le tocará a Drew Rasmussen, uno de los mejores abridores de la Liga Americana. Los Rays no han perdido una apertura de Rasmussen desde el 9 de julio, con marca perfecta de 11-0 en sus presentaciones desde entonces. Martínez lanzará con un día adicional de descanso, mientras que Rasmussen trabajará con cuatro días de descanso apenas por séptima vez esta campaña. El zurdo Ian Seymour y el derecho dominicano Freddy Peralta estarían alineados para abrir el miércoles y el jueves, respectivamente.
Yankees: Carlos Rodón y Max Fried abrirán los juegos de la doble-cartelera, en ese orden. Ambos han lidiado con lesiones esta temporada, pero están recuperando su mejor nivel en el momento indicado. En tres aperturas de septiembre, Rodón tiene marca de 2-0 con efectividad de 2.08, dejando atrás un episodio de inflamación en el codo izquierdo. Después de ingresar dos veces a la lista de lesionados por una contusión ósea en el codo de lanzar, Fried tiene récord de 1-0 y promedio de carreras limpias de 1.69 en tres aperturas este mes. Cole y Cam Schlittler, favorito para ganar el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, seguirán en el tercer y cuarto partidos de la serie, respectivamente.
¿Qué ha estado funcionando bien últimamente para cada equipo?
Rays: ¿Todo? Los Rays acaban de registrar récord de 8-1 durante su última estadía en casa de la campaña regular y han ganado cuatro series consecutivas contra los Bravos, Astros, Atléticos y Medias Rojas. Desde que fueron barridos en una serie de cuatro partidos en el Fenway Park tras la pausa del Juego de Estrellas, tienen marca de 39-18, la mejor de la Gran Carpa desde el 20 de julio. Su pitcheo abridor se ha visto particularmente sólido, con efectividad de 2.81 este mes, sólo detrás de la de los Yankees. Como de costumbre, han encontrado distintas maneras de anotar carreras, incluyendo ataques tempraneros como el del domingo y un par de jonrones para dejar en el terreno al rival por parte del candidato al JMV de la Liga Americana, el dominicano Junior Caminero.
Yankees: De repente, estos Yankees se encuentran apoyándose en la fortaleza de su pitcheo, confiando en que la ofensiva terminará respondiendo. Ben Rice conectó su 39no cuadrangular, la mayor cantidad del equipo, cumpliendo una predicción que Boone hizo durante los Entrenamientos de Primavera. Rice dijo que Boone estaba bromeando con él, quedándose con “uno o dos” por debajo de la cifra que él prefería, así que habrá que estar atentos a Rice mientras busca su 40mo vuelacercas esta semana. Austin Wells ha conectado tres bambinazos en sus últimos seis encuentros, mientras que el puertorriqueño Heliot Ramos ha volado la cerca en sus últimos dos partidos. Podría ser una pieza importante si los Yankees quieren hacerse sentir en octubre.
¿Cuáles son algunas áreas de preocupación que podrían convertirse en un problema esta semana o en la postemporada?
Rays: Muchos jugadores de los Rays han dado un paso al frente, pero el primer bate del equipo, el cubano Yandy Díaz, ha tenido un mes complicado, con línea ofensiva de .229/.286/.357 en septiembre. Él marca la pauta para la alineación, así que obviamente será importante que llegue en su mejor nivel a octubre. Y esto es realmente buscarle la quinta pata al gato, considerando que tiene marca de 3-0 con un salvamento y efectividad de 1.42 este mes, pero Bryan Baker, líder de Grandes Ligas en salvamentos, suma más bases por bolas (cuatro) que ponches (dos) en siete presentaciones durante septiembre. También necesitarán que sea dominante en la postemporada.
Yankees: Más allá del tirón en la pantorrilla derecha de Aaron Judge, un asunto que los Yankees están manejando como si fuera un secreto del estado, comienzan a surgir preocupaciones sobre el estado del bullpen. La velocidad de Brent Headrick ha disminuido y el relevista podría estar mostrando señales de fatiga después de liderar las Mayores con 79 presentaciones. Tim Hill no ha sido la máquina automática de provocar rodados de años anteriores. Michael Fulmer permitió un jonrón que decidió un juego en Arizona. Pero no hay un asunto más importante que demostrar que pueden ganar sin Judge, el motor alrededor del cual gira su ofensiva. Tienen marca de 48-41 sin él, comparada con 41-25 cuando ha estado en acción.

item.title: [mlb.com] ¿Judge estará listo? Las claves de los Yankees de cara a la postemporada

PHOENIX -- Varias latas de cerveza fueron vaciadas sobre la cabeza de Aaron Judge mientras el capitán de los Yankees permanecía en el centro del clubhouse de visitantes en el Target Field la semana pasada, rodeado de compañeros eufóricos que celebraban la clasificación del club a la postemporada.
Judge entrecerró los ojos por el ardor y les advirtió a sus compañeros: “Me las van a pagar”.
Aun así, no pretenden que ésa sea su última celebración, pues tienen un firme control del primer puesto del Comodín de la Liga Americana y el título del Este de la Liga Americana todavía está en juego.
“Siempre es bueno cuando puedes celebrar esos momentos durante una temporada”, dijo el manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone. “Mucha gente dedica mucho tiempo, esfuerzo y sudor. Obviamente, éste es apenas el primer paso de lo que esperamos sean muchos”.
Ahora que aseguraron su pase a la postemporada, ¿qué más les espera a los Yankees?
¿Cómo podría quedar el roster para la postemporada?
C: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez 
1B: Luis García Jr., Paul Goldschmidt
2B: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
3B: Ryan McMahon, Amed Rosario
SS: George Lombard Jr., José Caballero
OF: Cody Bellinger, Trent Grisham, Spencer Jones, Heliot Ramos
BD: Ben Rice
LA: Gerrit Cole, Cam Schlittler, Max Fried
R: David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Brent Headrick, Tim Hill, Clarke Schmidt, Michael Fulmer, John Schreiber, Will Warren, Carlos Rodón
Los Yankees utilizaron a 12 lanzadores y a 14 bateadores cuando recibieron a los Medias Rojas en la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana del año pasado, así que partiremos de esa misma premisa para el 2026.
Cole está programado para lanzar el miércoles contra Tampa Bay, mientras que Schlittler lo hará el jueves. Mirando hacia adelante, eso sugiere que Cole tendría un día adicional de descanso antes del Juego 1 de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, mientras que Schlittler estaría con su descanso normal.
Es posible que los Yankees estén alineando a Cole para abrir el Juego 1 y a Schlittler para el Juego 2. Hasta ahora, han preferido no decir mucho al respecto, salvo por la confirmación de Boone de que Cole realizará una apertura en la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana.
Rodón podría estar en el bullpen para la serie. En nuestra proyección del roster lo tenemos activo, mientras que el dominicano Luis Gil y Ryan Yarbrough figuran entre quienes quedarían fuera. Ryan Weathers trabaja para regresar como relevista, pero el tiempo juega en su contra. Si está saludable, podría ocupar el lugar de Fulmer o Schreiber.
Chisholm espera regresar esta semana para la serie contra los Rays tras sufrir un esguince en el pulgar derecho, mientras que Grisham ha mostrado mejoría y podría quedarse con un puesto en los jardines. De no ser así, Max Schuemann está entre las alternativas. Otro aspecto para seguir: ¿Podrían los Yankees incluir a Anthony Volpe en lugar de Rosario? Es una posibilidad que vale la pena considerar.
¿Cuándo comenzará la postemporada?
Si los Yankees terminan disputando la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, ésta empezará el 29 de septiembre. La Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana arrancará el 3 de octubre.
¿Contra quién jugarían los Yankees si la temporada terminara hoy?
En estos momentos, sería una revancha de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana del año pasado, con los Yankees recibiendo a los Medias Rojas en el Bronx. Los Yankees ganaron aquella serie dos victorias por una.
Este año, los Yankees tuvieron marca de 7-6 contra Boston.
¿Todavía pueden ganar el Este de la Liga Americana?
Sí, pero tienen un camino cuesta arriba. Los Yankees tienen por delante cuatro enfrentamientos directos con los Rays a partir del martes en el Yankee Stadium, incluyendo una doble-cartelera para abrir la serie. Tampa Bay domina actualmente la serie particular por 6-3, lo que significa que los Yankees necesitarían barrer para quedarse con el criterio de desempate entre ambos.
¿Quién abriría el Juego 1 por los Yankees?
Como se mencionó anteriormente, Cole está programado para lanzar el miércoles frente a Tampa Bay y Schlittler lo hará al día siguiente. Por lo tanto, Cole tendría un día adicional de descanso antes del Juego 1 de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, mientras que Schlittler estaría con su descanso normal.
Después de permitir siete jonrones en sus dos aperturas anteriores, Cole mermó las dudas externas sobre una posible apertura en los playoffs con una sólida actuación en Arizona. Fried y Rodón han lidiado con lesiones, pero están recuperando su mejor nivel en el momento indicado.
Warren realizará una apertura más durante la serie contra los Orioles, según Boone, pero llegará a los playoffs como una interesante alternativa para el relevo.
¿Será Judge un factor en los playoffs?
Los Yankees han sido poco específicos sobre el estado de Judge. Boone ha evitado ofrecer un plazo estimado para su recuperación e incluso revelar el grado del tirón en la pantorrilla derecha. En términos generales, hasta un tirón de Grado 1, el de menor gravedad, requiere de dos a tres semanas para una recuperación completa.
Es casi seguro que Judge intentará regresar antes. La primera fecha en la que podría ser activado sería para el Juego 162, el 27 de septiembre. Tal como está el panorama ahora mismo, existe una posibilidad muy real de que los Yankees no cuenten con Judge al menos para una potencial Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana.
Judge dijo que le “gustaría” estar activo para la postemporada y que ése es “el plan”, pero no dijo necesariamente que sería para el 29 de septiembre.
¿Cuáles son las otras preocupaciones en cuanto a lesiones?
Grisham ha avanzado en su programa progresivo de correr y debe de estar disponible para el roster de los playoffs, aunque Boone dijo que no será activado antes de que termine la temporada regular. Chisholm ha estado bateando y realizando tiros, y debe de ser activado durante la serie contra los Rays. Si sufre algún contratiempo, Volpe entraría en consideración.
Y aunque los Yankees no han descartado a Giancarlo Stanton, quien ha estado bateando, han ofrecido pocas novedades sobre su recuperación del más reciente tirón en la pantorrilla.

NEW YORK -- It has felt inevitable that the American League East race would be decided this week in the Bronx.
The Rays have led the Majors’ most competitive division for most of the season, and they haven’t ceded the top spot in the standings since reclaiming first place on June 27.
But the Yankees have always been there -- threatening and falling back, perhaps -- but never trailing by enough to diminish the potential importance of this week.
Well, here it is.
The Yankees will host the Rays in a four-game series at Yankee Stadium, beginning with a separate-admission doubleheader on Tuesday. Thanks to the Rays’ terrific homestand and the Yankees’ series loss in Phoenix, the question now is how much longer this race will remain alive.
The Rays arrived in New York holding a six-game lead in the division race with only seven games remaining. One victory by Tampa Bay will eliminate the Yankees from the AL East race and lock them into an AL Wild Card spot. So for the Yankees to have any chance, they must pull off a four-game, three-day sweep.
The stakes? As Gerrit Cole once said, “They’re high.” Let’s dive in.
What’s at stake?
Rays: Winning just one game will guarantee the Rays’ first AL East championship since 2021, giving them a bye through the Wild Card Series and home field advantage in both the AL Division Series and -- if they advance -- the AL Championship Series. They also need just one win to clinch the season series against the Yankees.
Yankees: Manager Aaron Boone acknowledges that it would be a “tall order” to keep the Rays from spraying bubbly in the Bronx, but that’s exactly what they intend to do. They entered the season looking to change the narrative after coming up short in their pursuit of the Blue Jays last year. They’re instead on the verge of settling for another consolation prize and needing to fight through a best-of-three.
How are the starting rotations lined up?
Rays: They will send their two best starters to the mound for Tuesday’s doubleheader. First comes veteran right-hander Nick Martinez, their clubhouse leader and most dependable source of innings. Tampa Bay has a 22-7 record behind Martinez this season. Then comes Drew Rasmussen, one of the AL’s top starters. The Rays haven’t lost one of Rasmussen’s starts since July 9, going a perfect 11-0 in his outings since then. Martinez will be pitching with an extra day of rest, while Rasmussen will be working on four days’ rest for only the seventh time this season. Left-hander Ian Seymour and right-hander Freddy Peralta would be in line to start Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.
Yankees: Carlos Rodón and Max Fried will start the doubleheader, in that order. Both have dealt with injuries this season but are rounding into form at the right time. In three September starts, Rodón is 2-0 with a 2.08 ERA, putting a bout with left elbow inflammation into his rear-view mirror. After twice landing on the injured list with a bone bruise in his pitching elbow, Fried is 1-0 with a 1.69 ERA in three September starts. Cole and AL Cy Young Award frontrunner Cam Schlittler follow in the third and fourth games of the series, respectively.
What has been going well for each team lately?
Rays: Um, everything? The Rays just went 8-1 during their final regular-season homestand, and they’ve won four straight series against the Braves, Astros, A’s and Red Sox. Since getting swept in a four-game series at Fenway Park coming out of the All-Star break, they’ve put together a 39-18 record -- the best in baseball since July 20. Their starting pitching has been particularly strong, with a 2.81 ERA this month that ranks second to only the Yankees. They have found different ways to score runs, as usual, including early rallies like Sunday and a pair of walk-off homers from AL MVP candidate Junior Caminero.
Yankees: These Yanks suddenly find themselves leaning on the strength of their pitching, believing the offense will eventually deliver. Ben Rice cracked his team-leading 39th home run, fulfilling a prediction Boone made in Spring Training. Rice said Boone was teasing him, coming up “one or two” short of his preferred total, so look for Rice to swing for his 40th this week. Austin Wells has hit three homers in his last six games, while Heliot Ramos has homered in his last two games. He could be an important piece if the Yankees are going to make October noise.
What are some areas of concern that could be an issue this week or in the postseason?
Rays: Plenty of Rays have picked up the slack, but leadoff man Yandy Díaz has had a tough month, with a .229/.286/.357 slash line in September. He sets the tone for their lineup, so it’s obviously important for him to be in top form come October. And this is really nitpicking, considering he’s 3-0 with a save and a 1.42 ERA this month, but MLB saves leader Bryan Baker has more walks (four) than strikeouts (two) in seven September appearances. He’ll need to be lights-out in the postseason, too.
Yankees: Other than Aaron Judge’s right calf strain, which the Yankees are treating like a top-secret matter of national importance, there are concerns bubbling about the state of the bullpen. Brent Headrick’s velocity has dipped and he may be showing fatigue after a Major League-leading 79 appearances. Tim Hill hasn’t been the automatic ground-ball machine of years past. Michael Fulmer gave up a game-winning homer in Arizona. But there’s no bigger issue than proving they can win without Judge, the engine around which their offense is built. They are 48-41 without him, compared to 41-25 with him.

item.content:encoded:
Shortly after getting walked-off by the Diamondbacks on Saturday night, the Yankees acknowledged their reality.
“Mathematically, [it’s] probably pretty tough, but you never know,” Cody Bellinger said of winning the American League East.
Unable to bounce back with an 8-4 loss in Sunday’s series finale against Arizona, the second-place Yankees are now six games back of the division-leading Rays with seven games left in the regular season. The rivals will play four of those games against each other at Yankee Stadium this week, starting with a doubleheader on Tuesday.
Aaron Boone acknowledged that his team will probably have to sweep the Rays just for a crack at the division crown, as FanGraphs gave the Yankees a measly 2.7% chance of winning the AL East before Sunday’s game.
“There’s still a chance,” Cam Schlittler said, “but we gotta play our asses off a little bit.”
While the Yankees still technically have a shot to defy the odds, the far likelier scenario is that their postseason begins on Sept. 29 at home against Boston in the Wild Card round for the second straight year.
With that in mind, let’s try to predict what the club’s roster could look like for that series.
Hitters (15): Ben Rice, Heliot Ramos, Spencer Jones, Trent Grisham, Cody Bellinger, Ryan McMahon, George Lombard Jr., Paul Goldschmidt, Luis García Jr., Jazz Chisholm Jr., José Caballero, Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez, Anthony Volpe, Amed Rosario
With the Yankees providing minimal info on Aaron Judge’s calf strain, it can’t be assumed he’ll be available.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. could return from a sprained thumb as soon as Tuesday. Meanwhile, Trent Grisham is still in play as a playoff option as he recovers from a hamstring strain, but Boone said that activating him before the end of the regular season is “complicated,” partly due to roster logistics.
With Max Schuemann presumably the corresponding move for Chisholm, the Yankees would have to option someone else if they activated Grisham before the playoffs. That someone wouldn’t be able to be recalled for 10 days barring a new injury; it seems like Jasson Domínguez is being protected from that window in case he’s needed for the Wild Card roster.
Grisham has been doing baseball activities and is “pretty deep into his running progression,” Boone said. If he is on the Wild Card roster, the Yankees will have an interesting decision to make between him and Spencer Jones in center field.
Third base could also be a conundrum, as Ryan McMahon and José Caballero don’t offer much offensively, and Amed Rosario is a poor defender. He’s only on the roster as an option against lefties, even though he hasn’t been great against them.
Another idea would be to use Volpe, who has been playing second, at third against lefties since he played a few games there in the minors this season. However, he doesn’t have a strong arm, and he hasn’t been working at third base since being recalled. Volpe said that the Yankees have not talked to him about manning the hot corner before the regular season ends.
“We’ll see,” Boone said. “First things first, getting Jazz back, and then we’ll figure out as the week unfolds how I want to play it.”
Volpe can also play second over Chisholm against lefties.
Pitchers (11): Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, Clarke Schmidt, John Schreiber, Tim Hill, Ryan Weathers
As things stand, Carlos Rodón, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Cam Schlittler are scheduled to pitch against the Rays, in that order. That would give Cole, who has struggled to get swing-and-miss, an extra day of rest if he were to start Game 1 of the Wild Card round. Schlittler, the AL Cy Young frontrunner, would be on regular rest if tabbed for Game 1.
Because the Wild Card round is a best-of-three series, Rodón isn’t needed, especially with Will Warren expected to work out of the bullpen and able to provide length.
Warren, slated to make one more start this season after struggling on Sunday, is one of a few converted starters who could impact the Bombers’ bullpen this postseason. Clarke Schmidt and Ryan Weathers are the others. Schmidt, being cautious in his return from Tommy John surgery, couldn’t come into Sunday’s game due to some bicep cramping, while Weathers isn’t expected to return from a flexor strain before the regular season ends.
Still, neither Boone nor pitching coach Matt Blake ruled out the idea of Weathers’ first game back coming in the playoffs.
“I don’t know if ‘comfortable’ is [the right word],” Blake said, “but it might be the course of action where he’s the best option even though he hasn’t pitched in the last three or four weeks.”
As for the relievers that the Yankees have leaned on all season, David Bednar, Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick headline the group. All have been used heavily, especially Headrick.
The lefty allowed a grand slam to Nolan Arenado and saw his fastball velocity down an average of 1.3 mph during his major league-leading 79th appearance on Sunday, but he insisted that he feels fine physically. Boone also downplayed concerns over Headrick’s ongoing velocity fluctuations, though he did say that he hopes to get him and other relievers “in a good spot” with some rest ahead of the playoffs.
That said, the Yankees still haven’t been eliminated from the AL East race. They’ll keep trying to take the division from the Rays until they are.
“We’re going to show up Tuesday,” Boone said, “and try and kick their butt.”

The final road game of the 2026 regular season is upon us, as the Yankees will conclude it with a seven-game homestand before likely hosting the Red Sox for the Wild Card Series. If the season ends there, this is the end of the line for the gray uniforms for 2026, but obviously, we all hope we'll see them next in Tampa (and more) in early October.
Looking to end a road slate that has been very generous to the Yankees on a high note is Will Warren, who's finishing his sophomore season strong after his great start to the campaign unraveled into a bit of a mess over the summer. Rotation reinforcements that threatened to throw him in the bullpen never came with the recurring injuries, so he'll finish 2026 with 30 starts for the second straight season. This is No. 29, as he enters with a 3.89 ERA (108 ERA+) and 4.07 FIP in 148 innings. No matter what happens from here, Warren has had a successful year in solidifying himself as a true MLB-caliber rotation arm.
Opposing him will be a former Cy Young winner trying to round into form off Tommy John surgery in Corbin Burnes, whom Yankees fans remember well from his lone season in Baltimore in 2024. Returning from a 16-month absence on September 8 to help with the playoff push, Burnes has allowed five runs across 7.2 innings with six strikeouts to two walks against the Royals and Marlins. He isn't totally built up, having thrown 75 pitches in his last start, so expect him to settle around 80-85 today. He's always befuddled the Yankees, pitching to a 1.93 ERA across 23.1 innings in his career, but he doesn't have a win in any of those four starts.
Ben Rice will once again lead off, followed by Cody Bellinger, Heliot Ramos, and Luis García Jr. We've seen better ABs and swings from George Lombard Jr. lately, who'll bat fifth. Spencer Jones is back after a one-day absence due to a sore foot and will bat in front of Anthony Volpe, Austin Wells, and José Caballero.
Lars Nootbaar will also be a repeat leadoff hitter for the D-backs, followed by Ketel Marte, Gabriel Moreno, and Geraldo Perdomo. Corbin Carroll is batting fifth, Nolan Arenado will bat sixth, and former Blue Jay Jesús Sánchez bats seventh ahead of last night's hero Pavin Smith and Tim Tawa.

Austin Wells has spent most of 2026 trying to climb out of a hole. His season line still carries the scars, but the past few weeks have looked a lot less bleak.
Wells went 2-for-3 with a homer and a walk in Friday’s loss to Arizona. Since Sept. 1, he has three homers, nine walks and a .772 OPS in 15 games. The Yankees cannot pretend that is meaningless with October approaching.
I do not buy the idea that three weeks erase a bad season. Wells has a .610 OPS overall, and any playoff decision has to account for the longer sample. But he is working counts, getting on base and putting a few mistakes in the seats again. He looks different from the hitter fans watched grind through much of the summer.
The Yankees have not solved catcher
The tempting move would be to call this a nice finish and keep the pecking order exactly where it was. That would miss the point. A club does not need Wells to become an All-Star in two weeks. It needs him to keep giving the lineup a real at-bat from a position that has been a drag far too often.
The catcher’s defense and handling of the staff will remain part of the equation. They should. Still, a second half that ends with better plate decisions and a little power makes the choice less automatic.
October should stay open for Wells
The Yankees do not have to hand Wells a postseason job today. They should keep running him out there while he is producing and see whether this run has another gear.
It is not a miracle comeback story. It is a late chance to turn a disappointing year into a harder decision, which beats entering October with no decision at all.

Field Level Media

20 Sep 2026, 13:49 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Arianna Grainey)
Pinch hitter Pavin Smith hit a two-run, walk-off homer with one out in the ninth and the Arizona Diamondbacks beat the New York Yankees 5-3 on Saturday in Phoenix on a night the franchise celebrated the 25th anniversary of their 2001 World Series victory over the Yankees.
Ildemaro Vargas walked to lead off the ninth off Michael Fulmer (0-1), reaching base after he appealed the 3-2 pitch that originally was called a strike. After a strikeout, Smith hit a 391-foot homer to right center for the D-backs' 46th comeback win of the season
Heliot Ramos and Austin Wells hit bases-empty homers for the Yankees, who had won four of five and eight of 10. Wells and Jose Caballero had two hits apiece.
Nolan Arenado had two hits and Jordan Lawlar added a two-run triple for the D-backs, who had lost three in a row and five of six.
The Yankees (89-65), who have clinched a playoff berth, fell five games behind Tampa Bay (94-60) in the American League East and remained 5 1/2 games ahead of Boston (84-71) for the top AL wild-card spot. The Yankees and Rays play a four-game series in Yankee Stadium beginning with a split doubleheader Tuesday.
White Sox 3, Tigers 1
Sean Burke hurled six quality innings and Miguel Vargas homered to help Chicago earn a victory over visiting Detroit.
Burke (10-7) allowed one run on five hits for Chicago, which remained a game behind American League Central-leading Cleveland. Sam Antonacci and Munetaka Murakami both drove in a run and Grant Taylor delivered a four-out save, his 10th overall this season.
Jackson Jobe (2-3) threw six innings of three-run, four-hit ball, striking out nine for Detroit, which remains barely alive in AL Central contention. The Tigers' wild-card elimination magic number is down to one. Kevin McGonigle drove in Detroit's lone run.
Mets 10, Phillies 3
Francisco Alvarez had two hits, including the go-ahead three-run homer in the fifth, as host New York routed skidding Philadelphia.
Carson Benge was 3-for-4 with a solo homer and two RBIs for the Mets. Brett Baty had two hits, including a run-scoring single, while Benge, Juan Soto and Bo Bichette each had RBI singles during a four-run eighth.
Alec Bohm had RBI singles in the fourth and fifth for the Phillies, who missed a chance to take over the top National League wild card, at least temporarily. The Cubs and Padres both won to remain tied atop the NL wild-card race.
Brewers 1, Orioles 0Robert Gasser pitched seven shutout innings as the first of three Milwaukee pitchers in a victory against host Baltimore.
It marked the second shutout for Milwaukee pitchers in an eight-game stretch, needing only four strikeouts for the latest accomplishment. The Brewers scored on Gary Sanchez's second-inning groundout to knock in Joey Ortiz, who tripled with one out.Baltimore has lost the first two games of the series following a three-game winning streak, further damaging its American League playoff hopes. Orioles starter Trevor Rogers (10-11) lasted eight innings, allowing one run and three hits.
Rangers 6, Blue Jays 2Texas won for the sixth time in its past seven games, defeating Toronto in Arlington, Texas.Rangers starting pitcher Cal Quantrill left the game after 1 1/3 innings with right lat tightness. Jordan Montgomery (1-0) replaced him and held Toronto hitless through 3 2/3 innings. Josh Jung gave Texas a 1-0 lead in the bottom of the first with a home run to right field.Jose Soriano (12-8) gave up six runs (five earned) on four hits and struck out eight in five-plus innings for the Blue Jays, who dropped to three games behind the Chicago White Sox for the final wild-card berth in the American League.
Rays 2, Red Sox 1
Richie Palacios produced a two-out, walk-off single in the ninth inning as Tampa Bay edged Boston in St. Petersburg, Fla., to even their final home series of the regular season.
Against Garrett Whitlock (7-2), Palacios looped a 1-2 sinker into right to score Junior Caminero as the Rays hit their third walk-off winner during their nine-game homestand. Jonathan Aranda homered while Liam Hicks and Chandler Simpson posted two hits apiece.

Nick Loftin had four hits, while Bobby Witt Jr. went 3-for-5 with two runs and extended his on-base streak to 17 games for the Royals. Carter Jensen hit a solo homer, while Jac Caglianone and Vinnie Pasquantino each had two hits for Kansas City.

Rookie Ethan Salas stroked an RBI single in the bottom of the 10th inning and San Diego edged visiting Miami.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Cam Schlittler se fue del Chase Field con otra actuación como lanzador que se consideraría dominante en casi cualquier otro sitio. Para los Yankees, fue otro recordatorio de que un as solo puede compensar hasta cierto punto cuando el margen a su alrededor no deja de reducirse.
Schlittler limitó a Arizona a tres hits y una carrera limpia en seis entradas el sábado por la noche, ponchando a seis y concediendo tres bases por bolas. Aun así , los Yankees perdieron por 5-3 cuando Pavin Smith conectó un jonrón de dos carreras como bateador suplente ante Michael Fulmer en la novena entrada, lo que convirtió un partido empatado en la undécima derrota de Nueva York en la última entrada de la temporada.
Con esta derrota, los Yankees quedan con un balance de 89-65 y a cinco partidos del Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, cuando solo quedan ocho partidos por disputar. Nueva York ya se ha asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero el camino hacia el título de división pasa ahora por cuatro partidos contra los Rays en el Yankee Stadium y necesitará algo de ayuda más allá de esa serie.
La actuación de Schlittler hizo que el resultado fuera más difícil de pasar por alto como una simple derrota de septiembre. Su promedio de carreras limpias bajó hasta 1,94, el mejor de la Liga Americana, y sus estadísticas de la temporada quedaron en 14-6, con 234 strikeouts en 190 2/3 entradas. Terminó su gira con un promedio de carreras limpias de 1,16 en 17 partidos como titular.
Los Yankees le dieron una ventaja momentánea de 3-2 en la sexta entrada gracias a dos jonrones solitarios de Heliot Ramos y Austin Wells. Schlittler empezó entonces la parte baja de la entrada con ocho bolas seguidas, Geraldo Perdomo conectó un sencillo de toque y un fly de sacrificio de Corbin Carroll empató el partido. Antes, un error de Schlittler en la defensa ante un toque de Tim Tawa ayudó a que Jordan Lawlar conectara un triple de dos carreras.
Juan Morillo se llevó la victoria tras lanzar 1 1/3 entradas sin permitir ningún hit con Arizona. Fulmer se llevó la derrota después de que Ildemaro Vargas ganara una revisión de ABS por una base por bolas al primer bateador en la novena y Smith mandara un cutter a las gradas del campo derecho. No hubo salvamento.
Así pues, Schlittler había sumado seis entradas más de excelente control de carreras sin cambiar el problema general de los Yankees. Nueva York acabó con un balance de 20-12 en sus 32 salidas como titular, un balance poco habitual para un equipo que solo ha encajado una carrera limpia o menos en 24 de esas salidas.
La racha histórica de no encajar carreras sigue adentrándose en un terreno cada vez más excepcional
La derrota no frenó el ascenso de Schlittler en las estadísticas. Según la investigación histórica de Sarah Langs, Schlittler acumuló 24 salidas en las que no permitió más de una carrera limpia, lo que le sitúa empatado con Bob Gibson en 1968 y Sandy Koufax en 1966 en el segundo puesto de la «Era de la Bola Viva». Koufax llegó a 25 en 1963.
En la historia de la Liga Americana, solo Walter Johnson logró más salidas de este tipo en una temporada: 27 en 1913 y 26 en 1914. El promedio de carreras limpias permitidas (ERA) de Schlittler a domicilio, de 1,16, solo queda por detrás del 1,06 de Johnson en 1913 entre los lanzadores de la Liga Americana con al menos 15 salidas como visitante.
Su trayectoria profesional es casi igual de impresionante. En sus primeras 45 salidas como titular en las Grandes Ligas, antes del sábado, Schlittler sumaba 312 strikeouts y una ERA de 2,24. Según los datos históricos que nos han facilitado, se sitúa junto a José Fernández y Paul Skenes como los únicos lanzadores que han superado los 300 ponches sin superar una efectividad de 2,30 hasta ese momento.
Schlittler tiene ahora una media de carreras limpias permitidas (ERA) de 2,22 en su carrera, con 318 strikeouts en 46 partidos como titular. Además, está intentando unirse a Ron Guidry en 1978 y a Spud Chandler en 1943 como los únicos lanzadores titulares de los Yankees de la «era de la bola viva» que han terminado una temporada con una efectividad por debajo de 2,00.
Schlittler lanza un mensaje contundente
No fue hasta después del partido cuando Schlittler pasó de hablar de sus propias estadísticas de lanzamiento a hablar de la posición de los Yankees en la clasificación. Cuando le preguntaron por la diferencia de cinco partidos, hizo un análisis directo de una carrera en la que Nueva York ha tenido varias oportunidades de recortar distancias.
«Tenemos que encadenar una buena racha. Va a ser duro. Creo que hemos tenido oportunidades durante toda la temporada para ponernos por delante, y no las hemos aprovechado muy bien. Así que todavía hay posibilidades, pero tenemos que darlo todo».
El mensaje cobró aún más importancia porque Schlittler acababa de asumir la responsabilidad de la jugada que le había cambiado el comienzo del partido. No utilizó las dos carreras no ganadas como excusa para que los Yankees perdieran otro partido que necesitaban ganar.
«Bueno, no diría que les di una oportunidad de verdad», dijo Schlittler. «Eso es culpa mía, así que asumo la responsabilidad. Cometí un error ahí y les dejé marcar dos carreras».
Reiteró esa idea unos instantes después, en lugar de echarle la culpa a la defensa, al bullpen o a la alineación.
«Bueno, así es el béisbol, pero sí, esa la pago yo».
Una jugada maestra más podría decidir cómo empieza octubre
Un gráfico comparativo de la MLB publicado antes del sábado situaba la temporada de Schlittler al mismo nivel que la de Clayton Kershaw en 2014, cuando fue MVP, y la de Justin Verlander en 2011, también como MVP. Esa comparación refleja hasta qué punto su candidatura ha ido más allá de la típica discusión sobre el premio Cy Young, aunque la carrera por el MVP siga siendo otra historia.
Para los Yankees, lo más importante ahora mismo es octubre. Los Yankees pueden armar su rotación para la postemporada en torno a Schlittler, que está listo para encabezar esa rotación, y Nueva York puede alinearlo para una salida más en la temporada regular, posiblemente contra Tampa Bay durante la serie de cuatro partidos que empieza el martes.
Su valoración sin rodeos después de que Arizona demostrara más que nadie la urgencia del momento. Los Yankees siguen contando con su mejor lanzador, que está rindiendo a un nivel histórico. Lo que sigue siendo una incógnita es si le han dejado suficientes partidos para dar un giro a la lucha por el título de división.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

NEW YORK -- Carson Benge had three hits to break Pete Alonso's Mets season rookie record, homering along with Francisco Alvarez as New York again prevented the Philadelphia Phillies from gaining ground in the National League wild card race with a 10-3 win Saturday.
Benge raised his hits total to 156, one more than Pete Alonso in 2019.
Alec Bohm had a pair of run-scoring singles and Bryce Harper delivered a sacrifice fly for the Phillies, who entered Saturday tied with the Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres for the three NL wild cards, five games ahead of the Arizona Diamondbacks.
Alvarez's three-run home run off Andrew Painter (3-10) put the Mets ahead for good in the fifth.
Benge doffed his cap to an ovation from the crowd of 37,468 following the record-breaking hit, an RBI infield single in the eighth.
CUBS 5, REDS 2 Matthew Boyd ended a six-start winless streak, Dansby Swanson hit his first home run since coming off the injured list and visiting Chicago moved closer to its second consecutive playoff berth by beating Cincinnati. Michael Busch hit a tiebreaking home run off Nick Lodolo (3-6) in the sixth inning for a 3-2 lead, reaching 20 home runs for the third time in four seasons. Swanson added a ninth-inning drive against Zach McCambley, his first since Aug. 12.
NATIONALS 8, CARDINALS 5 (11) Washington scored four runs in the top of the 11th inning to break a 4-4 tie, then worked out of a bases-loaded jam with no outs in the bottom of the inning to get by host St. Louis. Jose Terra hit a two-run double to break the game open, giving the Nationals a 7-4 lead. Dylan Crews' sacrifice fly scored Jacob Young to make it 8-4. JJ Wetherholt hit an RBI single in the bottom of the inning to provide the final margin.
AMERICAN LEAGUE
RANGERS 6, BLUE JAYS 3 Five relievers held Toronto to six hits after Cal Quantrill left 12 pitches in because of right lat tightness, and Texas moved into sole possession of the AL West lead for the first time since late August with a win over visiting Toronto. Texas has won six of seven and moved a half-game ahead of Houston, which holds the tiebreaker. The Rangers have a winning record for the first time since before play on Aug. 11.
WHITE SOX 3, TIGERS 1 Sean Burke pitched six effective innings, Miguel Vargas homered and Chicago topped visiting Detroit. The White Sox dropped at least 101 games in each of the last three years. They could become the first big league team to make the playoffs after finishing with at least 100 losses in each of the previous two seasons. Burke (10-7) allowed one run and five hits in his second consecutive win. Grant Taylor got four outs for his 10th save.
RAYS 2, RED SOX 1 Richie Palacios dropped a fly ball into shallow right in the ninth inning to score Junior Caminero and give Tampa Bay a victory over visiting Boston. The Rays, who've won seven of their last eight, capitalized on two fortuitous bounces in the ninth. First, Caminero's foul popup bounced off the Tropicana Field catwalk and out of the reach of third baseman Caleb Durbin. Caminero then lined the next pitch from Garrett Whitlock (7-2) into left. Three batters later, after Chandler Simpson singled, Connor Wong's passed ball moved Caminero to third.
GUARDIANS 12, ATHLETICS 6 Angel Martínez homered from both sides of the plate and had his second career four-hit game, Chase DeLauter had a three-run home run, and host Cleveland remained in first place in the AL Central with a victory over the Athletics.
INTERLEAGUE
BRAVES 6, ASTROS 3 Ronald Acuna Jr. hit a go-ahead grand slam in the seventh inning, and visiting Atlanta beat Houston to drop the Astros out of the AL West lead. Trailing 2-1, Atlanta loaded the bases against AJ Blubaugh (5-3) and Acuna homered off Bryan Abreu for his second grand slam this season and the fifth of his big league career. Acuna singled and walked twice in his first three plate appearances. He has homered in three of his last four games.
BREWERS 1, ORIOLES 0 Visiting Milwaukee tied a team record with their 97th win of the season, beating Baltimore with the help of a fly ball lost in the sun by Orioles right fielder Rece Hinds. Hinds lost Joey Ortiz's fly ball in the sun in the second inning and tumbled to the ground, and Gary Sánchez hit into a run-scoring groundout.
PIRATES 6, ROYALS 5 Brandon Lowe hit a go-ahead two-run home run in the eighth to lift host Pittsburgh to a victory over Kansas City. Lowe jumped on a pitch from Steven Cruz (2-4) and sent it into the seats in right field for his 33rd home run of the season, the second-most by a player in their first year with the Pirates.
ROCKIES 5, MARINERS 3 Host Colorado used a four-run seventh inning to earn a victory over Seattle. The Mariners built a 3-0 lead, thanks to a two-run home run from Cal Raleigh in the first and a solo shot from Randy Arozarena in the third. Cole Carigg hit a two-run single in the seventh that gave the lead to Colorado, which got an RBI single from TJ Rumfield to tie the game at 3-3 earlier in the inning.
DIAMONDBACKS 5, YANKEES 3 Pavin Smith hit a two-run home run to right-center field in the bottom of the ninth inning to give host Arizona a victory over New York. Jordan Lawlar's triple in the bototm of the fifth scored Nolan Arenado to give Arizona a 2-1 lead, but Heliot Ramos hit a solo home run in the sixth to tie the game at 2-2. Austin Wells hit a home run later in the inning, giving New York the lead, but Arizona tied the game in the bottom of the inning when Ketel Marte scored on Corbin Carroll's sacrifice fly.
